modules.title: Begin with a delivery, not a battle
modules.kicker: Original example · Opening a session

sections.title: What the party can see
sections.text:
A Candlebone Porter waits outside a rain-swollen warehouse door. Its parcel is dry beneath a folded cloak. It knocks, checks the address, then knocks again. Inside, a shopkeeper is trying to push a cabinet across the doorway. The porter’s published concept is a forgotten delivery, so give its insistence a subject: the parcel belongs to the shopkeeper’s former partner. The shopkeeper fears what accepting it would mean. Those motives can create an encounter before anyone draws a weapon.

Describe the parcel, the locked door and the repeated gesture immediately. Useful observations do not need to be withheld until someone succeeds at Awareness. The party still must decide which person to approach and what result they want.

sections.title: Make the first question small
sections.text:
DM: “It offers the parcel when you name the address. The shopkeeper tells you to leave it outside.” Player: “I want to know whether the parcel is dangerous.” DM: “How are you examining it, and does the shopkeeper permit you to open someone else’s delivery?”

That question distinguishes a physical inspection from a supernatural claim. Looking for wires or heat can be ordinary investigation. A capability that reads memories needs its actual access and conditions. The porter’s Necrotic Resistance does not make the parcel cursed. If an uncertain inspection matters, agree what success reveals and what an unsuccessful attempt changes before selecting the relevant check.

sections.title: Teach the changed situation
sections.text:
Suppose the party learns that the parcel contains a repaired instrument and an apology. They can ask the shopkeeper to accept it, offer to store it or seek its sender. An Influence result can address uncertainty about trust; it does not force forgiveness. The porter might accept a signed receipt from an authorized recipient, because completing its delivery answers its purpose. That is this situation’s decision, not a universal command that all undead obey paperwork.

If violence begins, use the porter’s actual record, including Driving Blow. Its tireless appearance supplies no unlisted immunity, additional reaction or second Main Intent. Keep the parcel and the people in the room relevant to the fight.

sections.title: Leave something worth returning to
sections.text:
End with a concrete change: the shopkeeper has the instrument, the porter has completed its duty, or the parcel remains disputed. Ask who is responsible for it now. The shopkeeper’s gratitude can lead to a useful introduction; their anger can make that contact harder. Neither response requires an automatic reward tariff.

For new players, recap one procedure they used: “You named an outcome, chose an approach and learned what your action changed.” Avoid turning the recap into a lecture about every primitive family. A modest resolved problem gives them a reason to try the next one, while the unanswered sender provides a natural continuation.

sections.title: Prepare the people who can answer
sections.text:
Give the shopkeeper three usable facts before play: the parcel arrived with a damaged label; the former partner once owned the instrument workshop next door; the porter has returned every evening since. Give the shopkeeper a present need as well: tonight’s supply delivery cannot enter while the porter occupies the doorway. These facts support several approaches without prescribing one solution.

DM: “The shopkeeper offers to pay if you make it leave.” Player: “Does anyone know who the parcel was for?” DM: “She recognizes the partner’s name, but she has never opened it.” Player: “Then we ask her permission to inspect the label before threatening the porter.” That ordinary request can establish access without turning a conversation into a compulsory check.

Compare the changed scenes. If the party finds the partner at the infirmary, the obstacle becomes a conversation or a delivery route through crowded streets. If they force the porter away, the shopkeeper regains access but the unresolved parcel remains. If they persuade the shopkeeper to store it temporarily, someone has accepted responsibility, with a clear duration or ending condition. Keep the signed-for delivery, the offered payment and the porter’s condition as separate facts. None requires a new delivery subsystem.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Candlebone Porter carrying its protected delivery; the parcel, destination and blocked route must remain visible. Its undead silhouette establishes a possible threat while the surrounding scene communicates a task that can be completed peacefully.

modules.title: The ford belongs to two lives
modules.kicker: Original example · Negotiation under physical pressure

sections.title: Give both claims weight
sections.text:
A caravan needs to cross before water rises. A Mossback Grazer stands over the shallow stones where its young are resting. The caravan master sees a dangerous animal blocking a road. The grazer sees a group approaching the only dry refuge. Neither interpretation is a complete description of the other’s intention.

Begin with visible evidence: small tracks behind the guardian, a damaged cartwheel, rising water and a bank wide enough to wait on. Tell the players where people can retreat. The grazer’s defender role suggests holding the ford, but its actual Anchored Stand and Bludgeoning Resistance determine mechanics. Its picture does not establish immunity to movement or an automatic attack against every approaching person.

sections.title: Ask what the plan promises
sections.text:
Player: “I wave food and try to lure it away.” DM: “Away from the crossing, or away from its young?” Player: “Just far enough to lead the cart past.” DM: “It watches the cart and turns back toward the young. What makes that approach safe from its point of view?”

The answer might involve moving the young to another refuge, waiting for them to leave, unloading the cart or finding a parallel crossing. Those are materially different proposals. A friendly gesture may open communication without settling the guardian’s concern. Do not ask for one generic persuasion roll and then decide afterward whether the whole herd relocates.

sections.title: Let preparation remove uncertainty
sections.text:
If workers lay a stable path to an equally safe bank and withdraw from the young, the guardian has new information. It may move voluntarily. If the alternative refuge is doubtful, a check can concern the credibility of the demonstration or the quality of the route. Say which question is uncertain. Do not charge the same success again as animal handling, persuasion and repair when those rolls would all resolve one unchanged fact.

If the party chooses force, preserve the prepared exits. Injuring the guardian can scatter the young into water and change the rescue problem. Establish that risk before commitment; it is not a secret punishment for declining your peaceful solution.

sections.title: Carry the decision forward
sections.text:
A safe crossing can make the caravan willing to wait at other contested places. A rushed crossing might preserve the goods while damaging the ford. Record what actually happened rather than assigning a blanket reputation score. People who saw the event can describe different aspects of it later.

Keep the monster’s creature budget separate from the caravan’s loads or the goods’ value. None of those numbers measures who has a stronger moral claim. This encounter can contain a serious objective, dangerous terrain and a strong creature without requiring a fight. The question for the next scene is whether the route remains usable and whom the party has agreed to protect.

sections.title: Record two different successful crossings
sections.text:
Before play, sketch the shallow crossing, the herd’s resting bank and a steeper downstream approach. Note what the caravan carries that cannot easily be moved: one damaged wheel, an ill passenger or fragile food. Choose one, rather than attaching every possible inconvenience. The herd’s need for shelter should be equally concrete; its young cannot use the exposed bank safely during the current weather.

Player: “We can move the carts downstream if the grazer leaves us alone.” DM: “The driver knows that route, but the damaged wheel may need support on the descent.” Player: “We shore it first and keep someone watching the herd.” That changes the task from removing the creature to preparing a crossing. The grazer’s actual behavior still determines how it responds to approaching people.

If the party escorts the caravan through the resting bank, record whether the herd was displaced and where it went. If they repair the downstream route, record the added work and the route now available to later travelers. Both can achieve the immediate goal. Their later consequences differ because the world changed differently, not because one approach earned a hidden difficulty label or a compulsory combat reward.

modules.imagePurpose: Place the Mossback Grazer between the ford and its young, with the caravan’s stranded cart visible on the facing page. The picture should explain its defensive motive and why a different route changes the encounter.

quickFacts.value: Safe passage and safe refuge

quickFacts.value: Young, tracks, water gauge, alternate bank

quickFacts.label: Outcome
quickFacts.value: A changed route or relationship, not necessarily a defeated monster

modules.title: A sense has a physical subject
modules.kicker: Original example · Sensory targeting

sections.title: Locate the actual contact
sections.text:
A Hollowbark Listener guards a buried shrine beneath a timber road. Its Substrate Echo grants tremorsense with its stated scope. A traveler on grounded stone and a traveler on a suspended rope walkway are different sensory situations. Start by describing those surfaces rather than declaring that the guardian “knows everything nearby.”

The Listener can have ordinary sight or hearing only as its record and circumstances support. Its title does not make it a historian, and the shrine does not give it free telepathy. Read the granted sense before deciding what it locates. Treat the 30-ft reference as part of that actual rule, not as permission to detect through every material in an unlimited buried network.

sections.title: State what has been learned
sections.text:
DM: “The trunk turns toward the footsteps on the stone approach.” Player: “Then it can see through the wall?” DM: “You have seen it respond to ground contact. That does not yet establish vision through a wall. What do you want to test?”

A player might stamp at a known point, throw a stone elsewhere or use the suspended route. Resolve the evidence honestly. If the published sense locates an eligible grounded target, that location can support a specific-target working within the rest of its permissions. Range still answers distance, not whether Stone Alarm can do anything the guardian wishes. A signal and an attack remain distinct results.

sections.title: Run a contest of approaches
sections.text:
Suppose the party wants to pass quietly while an ally draws attention from the far end of the path. Describe the competing noises and contacts. A distraction can create uncertainty without erasing a valid sense. A check can resolve concealment or interpretation under those circumstances; it does not switch off an acquired permission merely because the roll is high.

The Listener’s practical tactic is to alarm allies rather than pursue every intruder. That gives the party choices after discovery: stop and explain their purpose, withdraw before help arrives, interrupt a valid alarm or accept the changed confrontation. Do not invent an instant all-shrine response. Establish who can hear the actual signal and how they could reach the scene.

sections.title: Record a reusable sensory ruling
sections.text:
Write the material connection, observed source and located target in plain words. “Footsteps through the connected stone under the western approach” is more useful than “detected.” If the group later returns on a changed surface, revisit the circumstances rather than enforcing the old result mechanically.

The same discipline helps player-created blindsight, scent, scrying and aura reading. Ask what information the actual rule supplies and what would interfere. A sense can locate without identifying, identify a trace without locating its source or reveal an approximate area. Those distinctions make investigation possible while preserving the benefit the character bought. Nobody needs ordinary eyesight when another valid sense provides the required location.

sections.title: Prepare the alarm as a relationship
sections.text:
Write down who the Listener intends to warn, where those people are and what they would do after a warning. A creature detecting movement is only the beginning of that causal chain. Its actual Stone Alarm must reach an eligible recipient through its authored procedure; an ominous pulse in the description is not permission to alert every inhabitant of the region.

Player: “I hang from the bridge supports so I do not touch the floor.” DM: “That may change whether this tremorsense can locate you. The watchkeeper can still see the bridge from the window.” Player: “Then I wait until the keeper checks the far door.” The group has separated two information sources and made a plan addressing both.

If the alarm reaches the watchkeeper, prepare one response grounded in their duty: close the storeroom, investigate the vibration or call the nearby repair crew. If the party speaks with the Listener, the same watchkeeper might become a person who can authorize their visit. A successful bypass changes who knows the party arrived; a negotiated approach changes who permitted it. Neither grants universal invisibility. Keep those outcomes distinct when someone later asks why the door was found open.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Hollowbark Listener touching rooted stone beside a shrine; distinguish the connected ground from a hanging walkway. Use the picture to support the question of where its published contact-based sense applies, without treating decorative rings as a new radius.

quickFacts.label: Anchor
quickFacts.value: Read the granted sense and its substrate

quickFacts.label: Tactical change
quickFacts.value: An alarm brings actual allies, not automatic reinforcements

quickFacts.label: Record
quickFacts.value: What was sensed, where and through what

modules.title: A hidden creature is not a known target
modules.kicker: Original example · Choosing a spot under uncertainty

sections.title: Offer evidence without certainty
sections.text:
In a ruined observatory, dust shifts behind a cracked mirror. A Moonspoor Lynx has used its actual Still Camouflage. The party knows that something moved; they do not necessarily know the creature’s precise body position. Describe the fresh marks, the displaced glass and the sound. Do not require a roll to hear a sound you have already told them they heard.

Camouflage is not invisibility, and concealment is not total cover. Read the saved ability and the current surroundings. If someone’s applicable sense locates the lynx, use that information. If it supplies only an approximate source, say so. The distinction matters before anyone declares a specific-target attack.

sections.title: Make the alternative explicit
sections.text:
Player: “I blast the lynx behind the mirror.” DM: “You know the scrape came from the alcove. Your present information does not fix its body position. You could inspect from another angle or affect a known spot with a supported area expression.” Player: “I aim at the alcove’s floor.” DM: “That location is clear. What area does your construction actually affect?”

Agree the spot, recipients, delivery and uncertainty before resolving it. An area working does not guarantee that the hidden creature is inside. If the chosen floor is empty, do not move the lynx into it to reward the clever phrasing. If it is inside, do not move it away to preserve a planned ambush.

sections.title: Keep investigation useful
sections.text:
A companion can watch the exit while another shifts the light or asks for silence. Those actions have ordinary value even when they grant no numerical bonus. A purchased advantage applies only if its conditions fit. When opposing bias exists, cancel it before adding resolution dice; do not invent a permanent concealment disadvantage beyond the actual rule or agreed situation.

If the lynx leaves its concealment to attack, update what can now be perceived. Its ambusher label does not grant an automatic surprised round. Any optional surprise treatment belongs to the table’s explicit agreement and the facts of this scene. The players may have prepared specifically to prevent that opening.

sections.title: Let information change the objective
sections.text:
The animal may be hunting a smaller creature trapped beneath the lens, defending a nest or merely seeking a route out. Choose and reveal evidence that fits your situation. Finding that motive creates decisions beyond locating a body. Opening a quiet escape can end the encounter; protecting a scholar might require holding a particular doorway.

Record how the target was located and what the party learned. If a character later builds a sensing capability for similar ruins, that experience can explain the desired permission. It does not automatically award a new sense. Their extraordinary construction still needs its acquired ingredients, limits, price and table review. Investigation informs a build without replacing its ledger.

sections.title: Let one observation alter the search
sections.text:
Prepare a room with three concrete observations: a lens turned toward a dusty shelf, fresh disturbed dust beneath it and a loose curtain beside an open window. Decide which observations the Lynx actually caused. The window can be a plausible distraction without secretly being another creature. What matters is that the party can test a hypothesis against stable facts.

Player: “I watch the dust rather than guessing where the camouflage is.” DM: “You see a disturbance near the shelf, but the curtain moves separately in the draft.” Player: “I mark the shelf’s near edge for an area effect.” DM: “That gives you a known spot. We still need the effect’s actual shape and reach to establish what it includes.” The distinction lets uncertain targeting matter without making camouflage a blanket protection from every interaction.

After the area changes, describe new evidence: movement out of the dust, a displaced lens or no visible response. Do not promise a hit merely because the party guessed well, and do not move the hidden creature after the declaration to preserve suspense. If the Lynx escapes through the window, its chosen route changes the next pursuit. If the party locates it and offers food, the scene can become a bounded approach to an animal rather than an obligatory attack.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Moonspoor Lynx partly concealed among the observatory’s broken lenses. Include readable disturbed dust and an empty nearby alcove so the image separates evidence of presence from certain target location.

quickFacts.label: Distinction
quickFacts.value: Evidence of presence is not precise location

quickFacts.label: Alternative
quickFacts.value: A known spot with actual area access

quickFacts.label: Pitfall
quickFacts.value: Moving the hidden creature after learning the player’s choice

modules.title: Draw the path before rolling
modules.kicker: Original example · Projected delivery and cover

sections.title: Describe three routes
sections.text:
A Rainspout Artillerist occupies a drainage tower over a courtyard. The party can cross open paving, follow a broken railing or pass behind a solid storehouse wall. Its Deliberate Shot uses the actual saved construction. Tell the players which places the creature can see and where a projected path is obstructed. Height helps explain its position; it does not supply a free range extension or an additional attack.

Use the current projected-cover references: minor obstruction gives −2 accuracy, standard half cover gives −4, and total cover blocks the trajectory. Apply them to the path in question. Do not penalize every courtyard action merely because the scene contains walls somewhere.

sections.title: Resolve access before accuracy
sections.text:
Player: “I return fire from behind the storehouse.” DM: “Can you see it from there, and where does the shot travel?” Player: “I step to the corner.” DM: “That opens a path past the broken railing. The railing partly obstructs this particular projected shot.”

State the agreed obstruction before the attack. If a direct manifestation has valid targeting and its required permission, it does not use intervening projected-cover penalties. That does not mean any character can rename a bolt “direct” to pass through a wall. Delivery is part of the working’s actual behavior. Knowing the tower’s position also does not necessarily locate a creature that has retreated inside it.

sections.title: Change the scene with movement
sections.text:
Crossing to the pump house can create a better line, but movement remains part of the whole-round allowance. A Medium actor with 30 ft who spends 20 reaching the corner has 10 left, including any movement required by a later valid reaction. Advancing to another track gives no fresh 30 ft.

The Artillerist can reposition when a firing place becomes unsafe, using its actual movement and Climbing Speed grant. Do not secretly preserve a perfect firing line from every new location. If the players block the tower’s stair or force it behind machinery, describe the cost to its options. They have changed terrain, not merely reduced a resource bar.

sections.title: Give the tower a purpose
sections.text:
Perhaps the mercenary wants to keep a water valve open for a client, while the party wants to close it before a basement floods. Those objectives explain why either side might move instead of attacking. The valve, workers and stair access should be as clear as the archer’s silhouette.

At the next Council, describe the new paths and declared pressures. A collapsed railing might remove cover while making a crossing dangerous. A shut gate might block pursuit without stopping a direct manifestation that still has valid targeting. Apply each change to the relevant action. One simple path sketch can save many disputes because everyone can see the actual obstruction being discussed.

sections.title: Compare the same shot from three places
sections.text:
On your courtyard sketch, put a stone parapet between the tower and the central doorway, a narrow iron railing along the stair and an unobstructed lane beside the drain. These physical features can support different projected-cover judgments. Label the judgment after drawing the path, rather than assigning a permanent cover value to the whole courtyard.

Player: “I shoot from the doorway.” DM: “The parapet blocks that projected path completely.” Player: “Then I move onto the stair.” DM: “From that point the railing provides minor cover along your line; apply the relevant projected penalty.” Player: “Can I move farther to clear it?” DM: “You have used 20 feet of your 30-foot movement this round. Show me where the remaining 10 reaches.” The choices concern geometry and a known resource.

The same target may have total cover from one position and no intervening cover from another. If someone uses an eligible direct manifestation, resolve its actual delivery and sensory requirement rather than pretending the projectile travels the same lane. At the end, record positions and movement used. A clear drawing prevents the next track from quietly granting everyone a fresh approach or turning the railing into a universal defense.

modules.imagePurpose: Place the Rainspout Artillerist on its drainage tower, with a wall, broken railing and exposed courtyard shown from one clear viewpoint. Overlay only labels for the actual projected paths discussed in the text; the illustration must teach why two routes have different cover.

quickFacts.value: −2 accuracy on the relevant projected path

modules.title: One rescue, several dependent parts
modules.kicker: Original example · Main Intent and complexity

sections.title: Begin with a moving load
sections.text:
A freight platform has tilted over a loading pit. A Counterlift Atlas is holding one side with its actual Counterweight Lift. A worker is pinned near the edge; another is trying to stop crates from sliding. The Atlas is a protector, yet its machine-like command to “keep clear” can conflict with the party’s rescue attempt.

Give usable distances and surfaces before timing matters. Mark a sound anchor, an exposed walkway and the crate that blocks access. State that the platform is presently held, not permanently safe. The Atlas’s large shape and Vitality augment do not establish infinite lifting, invulnerability or an automatic rescue reaction. Read what its actual construction supports.

sections.title: Name the dependencies together
sections.text:
Player: “I climb onto the platform, free the worker and pull them back.” DM: “That is one rescue intent. Reaching the worker, releasing the trapped leg and moving them safely depend on one another. What keeps the platform steady while you do it?”

A companion might secure a line while the Atlas maintains its support. The group can place the dependent rescue in the appropriate track after reviewing its complexity. Do not assign a separate Main Intent in every track. Do not make the modest damage of a tool determine timing: the task’s dependencies, not its apparent power, explain where it belongs in the shared round.

sections.title: Resolve the intersection that matters
sections.text:
Suppose the Atlas fears that climbing aboard will overload its support and tries to bar the walkway. The party can explain the tether, change the load or oppose its blocking action. A clash concerns whose timing reaches the critical point first. A contest concerns directly opposed effort. Choose the actual question; rolling both without distinct uncertainties only adds noise.

If the tether is secured but the worker remains trapped, record those as separate changed facts. The first success does not automatically finish the whole rescue. Conversely, failure to free the leg need not erase the line already established. Keep established support available unless an actual event or ending condition removes it.

sections.title: Teach a partial success honestly
sections.text:
DM: “The worker is attached to the line, but the crate still pins their leg. The platform is holding. The Atlas says it can let one end settle if everyone moves to the safe side.” This gives the next Council a changed problem with a new option. It is clearer than “the rescue failed.”

When the worker reaches safety, decide what remains unstable. Repairing the loader, recovering goods and thanking the Atlas can become later tasks. The creature’s role changes with its purpose; it need not turn hostile to provide a climax. The useful record is who is safe, what supports the platform and what action could change that support.

sections.title: Make the unfinished rescue visible
sections.text:
Prepare the platform’s drawing with three named points: the braced corner, the trapped worker’s access gap and the control that lowers the opposite side. Decide which support is holding before the party intervenes. The Counterlift Atlas’s actual lift can be one contribution, while wedges, rope and people can provide ordinary work that their circumstances permit.

Player: “I pull the worker out while the Atlas lifts.” DM: “The lift first has to create a usable gap. The other corner remains on its damaged support.” Player: “Then my intent is to wedge that corner and reach the worker once the gap opens.” Clarify the dependency before assigning the appropriate track. Several described motions can form one coherent rescue, but describing them together does not make them simultaneous independent actions.

After a disruption, compare what truly failed. A broken wedge may remove support while the worker’s freed arm remains free. A missed pull can leave the gap open and the worker still trapped. A successful release may leave the platform unsafe for the person operating its control. Carry completed changes forward. This makes the scene legible: the players can choose the next useful intervention instead of repeating the entire rescue because one later step met resistance.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Counterlift Atlas supporting a tilted freight platform while a trapped worker and reachable anchor point remain visible. The composition should let the reader trace a rescue dependency from support to tether to evacuation, rather than depict an unrelated fight.

quickFacts.label: Intent
quickFacts.value: Reach, release and evacuate as one coherent rescue

quickFacts.label: Dependencies
quickFacts.value: Support, tether, access and actual load

quickFacts.label: Record
quickFacts.value: Preserve completed setup separately from unfinished rescue

modules.title: The last ten feet matter
modules.kicker: Original example · Whole-round movement

sections.title: Start with a route, not a range bonus
sections.text:
A Skyhook Corsair boards a moored airship to recover a stolen dispatch. The ship has a main deck, a raised helm and a narrow bridge to the dock. Its actual Flying Speed and carried hook explain an aerial approach. They do not make every hook throw a free movement action or turn its Return-Catch Throw into an unlimited boarding device. Read that capability before applying its title to a new result.

Place the people who matter: the pilot at the helm, a courier beside the bridge and a guard near the hatch. Give distances for the approaches the party can currently use. Height, reach and a safe place to land remain distinct facts.

sections.title: Spend one allowance across the round
sections.text:
A Medium party member has 30 ft walking Speed. They move 10 ft in Fast to take hold of the bridge rail, then 20 ft in Measured to reach the courier. Their ordinary walking allowance is spent. They do not receive another 30 in Heavy or when a reaction becomes available.

DM: “You can reach the courier with the remaining twenty. If you go there, ordinary walking movement is used for this round.” Player: “Then I will stay ten feet short and pass the dispatch instead.” That is a useful choice. State the remaining amount before a player relies on a route you know would exceed it.

sections.title: A response still has a route
sections.text:
If the Corsair cuts the dock line, a character may propose a valid independent reaction to catch a nearby person or interfere with the cut. The reaction needs its perceived trigger, immediate scope and any movement it actually uses. A spent movement allowance is not replenished by spending a reaction slot. An acquired movement rule or an agreed consequence can support an additional move; establish it openly.

Do not reduce every heroic idea to “no movement left.” Ask whether reaching is really required. A nearby rope, an already held line or an appropriate capability might change the approach. Ordinary handling still belongs to the actual task; it is not a secret catalogue of unlimited free actions.

sections.title: Keep the dispatch in the encounter
sections.text:
The Corsair wants a document, not necessarily the pilot’s death. Moving the dispatch to the dock can shift the pursuit. Showing that it is an empty decoy can change the negotiation. A party member who stays by the hatch may prevent a retreat even without attacking.

End the round by naming who holds the dispatch, where everyone stands, which line remains attached and whose movement and reactions were used. You can then describe the next Council without reconstructing an entire chase. Aerial imagery creates excitement; the small remaining-distance record keeps that excitement coherent when three people reach for the same rail.

sections.title: Draw a destination for every expenditure
sections.text:
Sketch the airship’s gangway, the dispatch chest and the Corsair’s nearest secure perch. Distances should explain whether ordinary movement reaches a useful place, not merely decorate a tactical map. A flying creature’s own actual speed does not enlarge a player character’s walking allowance, and a hook’s return behavior is not the same as transporting its wielder.

Player: “I use 10 feet in Fast to get behind the crate, then 20 in Measured to reach the chest.” DM: “Mark those endpoints. If the gangway is pulled before Measured, the second part will need a new viable route.” Player: “Can my reaction carry me over?” DM: “Describe the trigger and actual movement permission. The reaction does not restore your spent movement.” This keeps an interruption understandable without pretending the earlier movement never occurred.

If the gangway stays, the party’s intervention might be retrieving the dispatch. If it moves, their next choice could be keeping the ship alongside, establishing another route or abandoning the chest to save a passenger. Record the chest’s location and who holds it separately from who boarded. A chase becomes more engaging when each expenditure reaches a meaningful position and each changed route creates a decision, rather than another unpriced movement allowance.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Skyhook Corsair approaching an airship by its carried hook, with landing rail and retreat route clearly separated. The facing sketch can label the player’s 10-ft and 20-ft movements; the portrait does not substitute for either actor’s actual movement record.

quickFacts.value: 30 ft walking across the whole round

quickFacts.label: Example split
quickFacts.value: 10 ft in Fast + 20 ft in Measured

quickFacts.value: Who holds the dispatch and controls a usable exit

modules.title: A reaction is an opportunity
modules.kicker: Original example · Perceived triggers and rescue scope

sections.title: Let the warning be readable
sections.text:
A hanging bridge tears near its far anchorage. The Wingstitch Chirurgeon circles beneath the span; a merchant slips where the rope has frayed. Its actual Wing-Catch Descent supplies the relevant rescue behavior within its saved limits. Its support role does not allow every fall in the valley to be caught automatically.

Describe the first snapped strand and the merchant’s grip. People can act before the final fall if their intentions and timing permit it. Do not hide the entire failure behind a narration that ends with the victim already gone, then ask whether anyone wanted a reaction. The perceived triggering moment must be available to the people who can actually perceive it.

sections.title: Ask for an actual response
sections.text:
Player: “I use my reaction.” DM: “What do you do at the moment the rope slips?” Player: “I catch the merchant beside me.” DM: “You are within reach and have a free hand. That is the response we will resolve.”

A default independent reaction uses an available slot, a valid perceived trigger and immediate Complexity 0–1 with self/touch or a single target scope. The slot is not a purchased success. Catching can still meet uncertainty or interference. An authored grant can change response scope or capacity, but the group must identify it. The Chirurgeon’s actual capability should be read with the same care as the player’s proposed action.

sections.title: Resume from what changed
sections.text:
Suppose the merchant is caught but the bridge continues tearing. Resume the triggering event from that changed fact. The rescue has not repaired the anchorage or transported the entire caravan to safety. A companion’s Main Intent can now secure the merchant while the Chirurgeon handles an eligible descent.

If two people respond to the same fall, decide which actions intersect. One might attach a tether while another takes the weight. They do not automatically earn two Main Intents because a shared event has several participants. Nor must both responses be discarded as redundant: their actual results can complement each other if the scope and timing are coherent.

sections.title: Make future risk different
sections.text:
After rescue, the damaged bridge remains damaged. Mark the torn rope, the merchant’s current position and any agreed injury or restriction. The next person crossing should not face an identical invisible surprise. Workers can install another line, unload a wagon or seek another route.

At the next Council ordinary reaction availability refreshes, but consequences do not silently disappear. If the merchant’s shoulder was injured, state its actual effect and recovery condition. Rescue scenes become satisfying when success creates a safer or more intelligible situation. Repeatedly dropping the same person to consume another reaction makes the ability feel like a tax rather than a meaningful intervention.

sections.title: Prepare the moment before the fall
sections.text:
Put the rescuer, the merchant and the nearest stable landing place on the bridge sketch. Decide what can be perceived before the line snaps: fraying rope, the merchant’s stumble or the sudden loss of the plank. Those observations establish why a character can respond. Do not retroactively announce an invisible trigger after the event has fully resolved.

Player: “When the plank gives way, I catch the merchant.” DM: “You can perceive that break. Is the merchant within the actual reach of your chosen response?” Player: “Not from here; I move closer beforehand and keep my hands free.” That preparation changes a later opportunity without guaranteeing success. When the trigger occurs, resolve the actual catch, its eligible complexity and any meaningful opposition.

A successful catch can leave both people hanging from a strained handhold. Reaching the safe landing remains a separate physical problem. A failed attempt can leave the rescuer holding the merchant’s bag, knowing their direction of fall or needing immediate help, depending on what was attempted and resolved. State the actual result rather than automatically turning every partial rescue into another full fall. Afterward, the Chirurgeon’s own contribution stays bounded by its record, and other characters retain the consequences they actually incurred.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Wingstitch Chirurgeon close enough to catch one falling companion while a second person stands farther along the damaged span. This relationship makes eligible immediate scope visible; avoid depicting universal rescue of every airborne creature.

quickFacts.value: A fall the responder actually perceives

quickFacts.value: One slot; immediate Complexity 0–1; eligible scope

quickFacts.value: Bridge damage and agreed consequences remain

modules.title: Control should change a choice
modules.kicker: Original example · A prepared predator’s terrain

sections.title: Prepare places worth choosing
sections.text:
A Sinkhole Maw has prepared an unstable hunting ground around a buried pumping station. There is a sound stone ledge, a ladder through a narrow shaft and an exposed cart ramp. Its Gravity Anchor Trap can control an eligible place according to its actual construction. Burrowing Speed supplies a route through ground; neither rule turns the entire ruin into unavoidable damage.

Describe fresh cracks, displaced rubble and a repeated dragging mark near the ramp. Each exit offers something different: the ledge is stable but farther from the trapped worker, the shaft is narrow, and the ramp gives a direct approach. Those differences are physical facts, not a menu of arbitrary bonuses.

sections.title: Name the controlled area
sections.text:
DM: “The loose gravel settles toward one marked patch beside the breach.” Player: “Is the whole floor pulling us?” DM: “The visible effect is centered there. You can inspect its extent or choose a route that avoids that patch.”

Read the saved trap’s recipients, placement, continuation and resolution. If the party crosses its actual boundary, apply the established procedure. If they bypass it, respect the bypass. Do not extend the effect secretly because the predator would otherwise lose its prepared advantage. A strong control ability remains useful when it protects an objective or forces a changed route; it need not cover every possible approach.

sections.title: Let opposition depend on opportunity
sections.text:
The Maw wants prey near its breach. A party member who climbs the shaft may be inaccessible to a close attack while remaining vulnerable to another actual hazard. A character on the ledge might draw it out. Read where the creature can travel and what working it can perform after that approach. Its Solo label does not grant extra independent actions.

If one actor tries to pull a worker clear while the Maw tries to anchor that same worker, the group can examine a directly opposed effort. If the question is reaching the worker before the predator, it is timing instead. Distinguish the two so control does not become a vague permission to cancel any rescue.

sections.title: Reward a changed hunting ground
sections.text:
The party may evacuate the station, brace a path, interrupt an eligible trap source or bait the Maw into open ground. Each changes the encounter’s relationships. Removing the worker from the breach can complete the objective even if the creature remains alive. Destroying a support might expose a safer path while making later repairs necessary.

Keep the creature’s base budget and separate equipment figure in the appraisal. Do not translate successful terrain use into an invented difficulty category. The useful review asks which routes the party understood, what they changed and whether the control effect was applied within its actual limits. A predator’s prepared terrain should teach attention, not punish every unanticipated plan.

sections.title: Prepare the control as an invitation to adapt
sections.text:
Give the pumping station three routes with different visible needs. The shaft is narrow and difficult to reach with a load; the ramp is broad but crosses the unstable ground; the ledge avoids that ground but passes close to the Maw. These are physical descriptions, not fixed skill requirements. A player may make the shaft usable by changing the load or find a way to support the ramp.

Player: “We send the injured worker down the shaft first.” DM: “Their splint catches on its narrow entry. What changes that obstacle?” Player: “We remove the loose grille and lower them in the sling.” The plan addresses a particular fact. If the Maw interferes, resolve its actual threat against the exposed work rather than charging an automatic damage toll for selecting that route.

Compare two resulting maps. If the ramp collapses after evacuation, the survivors are safe but their supplies remain above. If the ledge becomes secure, the station retains a useful access path while the creature occupies the lower floor. Write the changed terrain down. A control creature earns its place when the party revises position, timing or means; it need not deny every alternate route to remain a serious presence.

modules.imagePurpose: Place the Sinkhole Maw below a cracked hunting floor, with three visibly different exits around its breach. The artwork should telegraph disturbance and likely approach; mark any actual trap boundary only from its saved definition, not from dramatic cracks.

quickFacts.label: Control goal
quickFacts.value: Keep eligible prey near a breach

quickFacts.label: Readable choices
quickFacts.value: Stable ledge, narrow shaft, exposed ramp

quickFacts.label: Pitfall
quickFacts.value: Expanding the trap after players find a valid bypass

modules.title: A support creature needs someone to support
modules.kicker: Original example · Role through relationships

sections.title: Start with the injury
sections.text:
A Briar Covenant Tender protects a grove after a charcoal crew has cut into its roots. Its defender companion has been hurt; a young tree leans over the path. The Tender’s Splint and Rally is its actual support working. Poison Resistance belongs to its own record and does not automatically become an aura for every ally.

Tell the party what they can plainly see: a binding around the defender’s leg, an abandoned saw and a route around the sapling. A support creature becomes interesting when its work has a subject, a position and a reason to continue. “It heals the enemy every round” is too broad unless the actual construction establishes that behavior.

sections.title: Read the contribution before using it
sections.text:
Identify what Splint and Rally changes, whom it can affect, its range, its uncertainty and its ending terms. Use only that contribution. A descriptive bandage can help the reader understand the scene, but it cannot supply extra Vitality or remove a consequence the rule does not address.

Player: “Can I explain that we did not cut the roots?” DM: “The Tender can see you put the saw down and move away from the sapling. It still fears another crew. What are you offering to do about the damage?” A conversation can change the support relationship by changing whom the Tender sees as a threat.

sections.title: Give intervention more than one meaning
sections.text:
A hostile party might separate the Tender from its defender through an actual barrier or force it to retreat from an exposed position. A cooperative party can protect its treatment, repair a mundane support or retrieve supplies. Each approach affects who can reach whom. Do not reduce “interrupt the support” to compulsory damage when moving its recipient or changing its purpose can matter.

If the work has an ongoing requirement, state it at the agreed continuation point. Ordinary upkeep can be a restriction or task. Do not add the unresolved damage-triggered Vitality repayment scheme. A hit matters through its actual injury, interference and the construction’s terms, not through an invented universal cancellation rule.

sections.title: Let the grove remember specifics
sections.text:
Afterward, the Tender may know that one character carried the injured companion and another threatened the sapling. Keep those distinct observations. A later invitation to the grove can belong to the helpful person without granting the whole party a permanent friendship bonus.

The charcoal crew might also have a legitimate need for fuel. That can become a separate negotiation about a safer source. Supporting one injured defender has then opened a larger situation without requiring the Tender to become an all-knowing quest giver. Its mechanical role remains narrow; its relationships provide the broader adventure. That separation is useful whenever a creature’s support identity is stronger than its attack profile.

sections.title: Give support a visible opportunity cost
sections.text:
Prepare a grove diagram with the wounded defender beside one sapling and the charcoal crew working near another. The Tender cannot be assumed to support both locations without the actual reach, recipients and timing of its capability. Its desire to protect the grove can make where it stands a meaningful choice.

Player: “I show it that the crew’s fire is moving toward the second tree.” DM: “It sees the smoke. The defender still needs help here.” Player: “We offer to move the defender into shelter while it tends that tree.” The offer changes who can perform a task. It does not require an automatic social roll when the Tender understands, wants the proposed outcome and has reason to trust the exchange.

If the party instead prevents the support working, record what the defender actually loses or fails to receive. Do not erase previously resolved healing or protection merely because its source changes position unless that rule is genuinely continuing. If cooperation succeeds, the Tender may share access to the grove but retain a condition about fire or harvesting. A support role can create relationships and responsibilities as well as combat choices. Record which support ended, which completed benefit remains and what promise was made.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Briar Covenant Tender attending an injured grove defender, with the threatened sapling between them and approaching visitors. The illustration explains a support relationship and a protection objective rather than treating the Tender as a generic magical healer.

quickFacts.value: A particular injured defender

quickFacts.label: Actual support
quickFacts.value: Apply Splint and Rally as written

quickFacts.label: Alternate objective
quickFacts.value: Protect treatment or repair the threatened grove

modules.title: A firing lane can be the objective
modules.kicker: Original example · Ranged pressure and repositioning

sections.title: Explain the warning signal
sections.text:
A Cloudglass Harrier patrols a drifting ruin where visitors have moved a survey marker. Its Coded Eye Beam and flight let it signal or act through its actual saved behavior. Its role is ranged, but its beam’s name supplies no free communication language, unlimited split targeting or knowledge of every trespasser’s intent.

Begin with the marker, the open gap between towers and a sheltered crossing below. The Harrier signals before approaching; visitors can respond if they understand or investigate that signal. Choose what the guardian wants in this example: restore the marker and keep the ruin’s crossing clear. A visible request can make a later attack intelligible without making it inevitable.

sections.title: Put information beside danger
sections.text:
DM: “The beam repeats against the displaced marker, then the open gap.” Player: “Is it aiming at us or asking us to move?” DM: “You can see the sequence and where it points. Interpreting the code is still uncertain. How do you answer?”

The party can return the marker, present a known signal, inspect older marks or seek shelter while studying. A suitable check can concern interpretation; failure need not erase the observed sequence. Give an incomplete answer or a changed opportunity consistent with the agreed stakes. Do not use misunderstanding as permission for an unannounced unavoidable attack.

sections.title: Reposition with consequences
sections.text:
If the confrontation becomes timed, use the Harrier’s actual movement and line. It can leave one perch, but a new perch may place the marker beyond its view or expose its approach. A party member who carries the marker into shelter changes what can be targeted or observed. The beam does not bend around every obstruction merely because the monster is aerial.

The group might cross while another character demonstrates that the marker is being restored. Their Main Intents can depend on the guardian’s response. Resolve the actual timing or effort intersection. High ground and flight are circumstances to understand, not automatic additional reactions or an initiative advantage imported from another game.

sections.title: End when the lane’s use changes
sections.text:
An encounter can end when the crossing is safely occupied, the marker is restored or the guardian permits passage. Record which result occurred. If the party destroys the marker, the ruin might lose a useful warning function; describe that consequence only if it was a real established feature.

The ranged creature’s picture can make the location memorable, but the crossing is the tactical subject. Keep its position legible when you speak: “It now guards the eastern gap; the lower bridge is clear.” Players can then choose a route without demanding a full technical diagram every time. The same method works for archers, spotters and creatures whose attacks protect machinery rather than simply chase targets.

sections.title: A signal can carry a narrow truth
sections.text:
Prepare the drifting ruin with two firing perches and one damaged marker. Decide what the Harrier’s Coded Eye Beam actually communicates, who knows that code and which direction needs a clear lane. The party seeing a beam is not the same as the harbor receiving or understanding its message. These steps offer useful interventions.

Player: “I copy the flash pattern with a lantern.” DM: “The lookout recognizes lantern signals, but you have not yet learned this code.” Player: “Then I study the repeated pattern while someone repairs the marker.” That can separate a knowledge task from physical work. Whether a check is needed depends on actual uncertainty, available evidence and time; the scene does not supply a universal codebreaking cost.

When the ruin rotates, compare the lanes again. A working beam may no longer reach its recipient, while a previously hidden repair panel becomes accessible. Keep the creature’s position and the ruin’s movement visible. Success can restore a safe crossing without defeating the Harrier. Failure to send one signal can create a delayed warning or a boat taking the wrong channel rather than automatically ending the entire adventure. Those changed circumstances give the next Council specific work to address.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Cloudglass Harrier aligned with a clear gap between drifting ruin towers. The gap, shelter and moving platform should matter as much as the creature, making a beam’s usable lane and an alternate crossing visible.

quickFacts.value: Restore a marker and protect a crossing

quickFacts.label: Ranged question
quickFacts.value: Where is the actual lane from the current position?

quickFacts.label: Changed outcome
quickFacts.value: Safe crossing, restored signal or a lost warning function

modules.title: A solo threat is not a second rulebook
modules.kicker: Original example · Threatening a place as well as people

sections.title: Give the giant a destination
sections.text:
The Walking Foundry enters a working district seeking fuel. A coal yard lies beyond a crowded street; a disused kiln offers another source. Its actual Cataclysmic Shockwave can create severe pressure within its saved rules. Fire Resistance does not imply immunity to every industrial hazard, and a huge illustration does not grant unlimited reach.

Describe its route, the warning before its large working and the people who can still leave. The party’s first task might be evacuation rather than attacking. An enormous opponent becomes easier to run when its next destination is clear. It becomes harder when the DM invents a different unlisted answer to every player intervention.

sections.title: Review what the record really gives
sections.text:
Use its chosen creature budget in appraisal and calculate Item BU separately. A large base budget does not grant more independent Main Intents, extra reactions or automatic resistance to control. Read the actual acquisitions and work from them. If the solo needs a new mechanic, author and review that mechanic before relying on it in play.

DM: “It is turning toward the coal yard. The warning pulse is building along the street.” Player: “Can we lure it to the old kiln?” DM: “That addresses its fuel need. What shows it the kiln is usable, and what happens to the people along that route?”

sections.title: Let the party divide useful jobs
sections.text:
One actor can open a route, another can move workers and a third can interrupt an eligible part of the Foundry’s working. Place their actions by dependencies. They do not need a special objective-point subsystem: “the western gate is open” and “the last cart has cleared the street” are real changed facts.

Telegraph the shockwave’s actual scope before resolution. If the party moves outside an eligible area, honor that position. If a barrier changes a projected path, apply the relevant obstruction rules. Do not make damage inevitable to preserve the creature’s dramatic scale. A giant threat can remain frightening while the players’ correct preparation prevents a particular injury.

sections.title: Make ending more than destruction
sections.text:
The Foundry might stop at the kiln, exhaust its available fuel, accept a maintained safe route or be defeated. Each ending leaves a different district. A surviving machine can become a negotiated danger; broken streets can create repair obligations; a destroyed coal yard can threaten later heating.

State those consequences from actual events rather than attaching a generic failure surcharge. If the party chose the old kiln, show what that choice preserved and what it endangered. Their success is not smaller because they avoided fighting the solo. The encounter has tested coordination, information, access and consequences through a single visible purpose, using the shared rules the group already knows.

sections.title: Prepare a threat the town can respond to
sections.text:
Put three town facts beside the Foundry’s actual record: the kiln road is wide enough for it, the crowded market is not evacuated and the bridge can carry carts but may not bear the creature. Choose what its next movement threatens from those facts. Do not turn every street into a lethal hazard merely because the portrait looks immense.

Player: “We draw it toward the old kiln.” DM: “What can it perceive there, and why would it follow?” Player: “The remaining fuel is stored beside that road. We clear the carts and expose it.” If the creature’s behavior supports that attraction, the plan has a real lever. It still requires the people, route and timing to cooperate.

If the diversion succeeds, the market may be safe while the kiln needs containment or negotiation. If it fails, the evacuation effort can still save people and leave clear lanes for the next intervention. Record these partial achievements. A solo threat can remain impressive through its actual output, scale and the consequences of its choices. Giving the whole town usable tasks creates more participation than silently granting the creature additional turns whenever several players make progress.

modules.imagePurpose: Use the Walking Foundry at a scale that shows nearby occupied streets and a fuel route. Its body should dominate the spread while clear evacuation paths and the fuel destination remain visible, supporting a solo objective beyond reducing its Vitality.

quickFacts.value: Actual grants; no extra actions from a role label

quickFacts.value: Fuel route, warning pulse and occupied streets

quickFacts.value: Diversion or evacuation can resolve the objective

modules.title: Breathing, rescue and recovery are different
modules.kicker: Original example · Underwater pressure

sections.title: Prepare a reachable person
sections.text:
A cellar floods while its inhabitants search for a missing child. An Airshare Nautilus carries a breathing apparatus and can use its actual Breath Share. It is a potential ally, not a general exemption from underwater danger. Establish the stair, a submerged doorway, the remaining pocket of air and how the party locates the person beyond it.

The breathing working has recipients, scope and conditions. Read them. Its Swimming Speed does not automatically let a passenger match that speed or turn every rescue into immediate success. A person who can breathe may still be trapped, injured or unable to find the exit. Those are different problems with different possible approaches.

sections.title: Make the rescue sequence intelligible
sections.text:
Player: “The Nautilus gives them air, so they are fine.” DM: “They can receive the breathing support as written. Their leg is still beneath the fallen shelf. What frees it, and how will you get them to the stair?”

Use the shared round if freeing, supporting and moving the person have meaningful dependencies or interference. Ordinary lifting can be an eligible approach when the load and access permit it. A capability may change the shelf, but an impressive description does not add an unpurchased domain. Keep the rescue’s uncertainties distinct. One success to share breath should not silently heal an injury or complete the evacuation.

sections.title: Do not replace dying with a rest
sections.text:
If someone has collapsed at zero Vitality, they need actual rescue. Successful stabilization halts dying without automatically supplying Vitality or consciousness. Healing above zero normally ends dying and restores consciousness unless another consequence prevents it. Breath Share alone does not claim either result unless its actual rule explicitly provides it.

Once safe, the group can agree whether the circumstances earn a short rest. For a character with maximum Vitality 13, the ordinary short-rest allowance is 7 after upward rounding. At 10/13, restoring 3 reaches full and leaves 4 for later eligible short rests. Merely remaining in shelter does not spend those remaining points, and an agreed long rest heals independently and refreshes the pool.

sections.title: Leave the flooded place changed
sections.text:
Rescued residents can identify where the water entered. A door the party forced open may now let it spread; a diverted channel may protect one room while threatening another. Give those physical consequences clearly, rather than retroactively charging a damage price for the breathing assistance.

The Nautilus can become someone to protect while the party works on the source of flooding. Its limited contribution stays valuable because it answers a real need. A support creature does not require a broad healing aura to matter. The record at the end should state who is breathing, who is conscious, who remains trapped and which recovery or treatment actually occurred.

sections.title: Prepare two people with different needs
sections.text:
Give the child a trapped leg and the older resident a reliable memory of the cellar’s former doorway. Their needs and contributions differ. The child may need release and breath; the resident may be able to guide a rescuer but be unable to carry anything. This makes the scene more informative than a row of identical drowning targets.

Player: “We take the resident out first because they can explain the route.” DM: “They know the doorway, but moving them now leaves the child waiting beside the rising water.” Player: “Then one of us listens while the Nautilus stays with the child.” That distributes attention and support. Decide what the actual communication and breathing rules permit before the shared round begins.

If the child is freed while the exit floods, the party has solved one problem and faces another. If the resident reaches shelter, their route information can still help people inside. Preserve that information after a setback. At the end, describe the injured person’s remaining treatment need rather than assuming safety restored all Vitality. A later short rest can use the actual remaining allowance, while the flooded cellar and the rescuers’ separate consequences remain part of the situation.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Airshare Nautilus beside a flooded stair and a conscious stranded person, with the breathing apparatus prominent. Use the facing situation diagram to distinguish reaching the person, sharing breath and reaching shelter; do not imply the creature restores Vitality by proximity.

quickFacts.value: Breathing, release, evacuation, stabilization and healing

quickFacts.value: Maximum 13; allowance 7; heal 3; retain 4

quickFacts.label: Long rest
quickFacts.value: Agreed recovery is independent of the short-rest pool

modules.title: A scent is evidence, not a verdict
modules.kicker: Original example · Investigation and social consequences

sections.title: Give the clue a provenance
sections.text:
A Bellwatch Hound follows the scent of a missing courier. Its handler reaches a potter wearing the courier’s coat and accuses them of abduction. The party can see clay on the coat, a broken fastening and a parcel under the potter’s bench. The potter says the courier traded the coat for shelter the night before.

Scent Pursuit follows its actual rule. It does not automatically identify guilt, recover every event involving the scent source or distinguish an innocent exchange from theft. The handler can sincerely trust the hound and still interpret its result badly. That disagreement gives the party an investigation with immediate human stakes.

sections.title: Resolve the proposition being tested
sections.text:
Player: “I ask the hound whether the potter is lying.” DM: “The hound’s trail concerns the scent. It has not shown an ability to judge testimony. You can inspect the coat’s history through available evidence or use an actual information working that supports the question.”

A suitable check might address whether the potter’s account fits the observed timing, not whether every part of their life is honest. Give ordinary evidence freely when it is accessible: the shop’s neighbor saw a traveler; the kiln was warm; the parcel bears a name. Preserve uncertainty where facts remain missing. Do not make one failed interview erase all these independent sources.

sections.title: Give accusations an actual consequence
sections.text:
If the party publicly threatens the potter, their later request for help can meet distrust. State what changed: the potter refuses unsupervised entry to the workshop until the accusation is corrected. That is a concrete restriction with an ending condition, not a blanket numerical penalty to every social check in town.

If the party explains the difference between scent and guilt, the handler may agree to follow the coat’s earlier route. A credible explanation can change the decision without rolling. If trust remains uncertain, select that uncertainty and its stakes. Do not turn Influence into mind control; people can accept evidence while remaining angry about how they were treated.

sections.title: Keep more than one explanation alive
sections.text:
The courier might be hiding from a creditor, tending an injured friend or deliberately spreading false trails. Choose facts that support your situation, then let the party compare them. An unexpected theory should not force every prepared clue to become a lie; equally, it should not become true merely because it was clever.

Record who saw which evidence and who heard the accusation. Later witnesses can respond to their actual knowledge. The hound remains a useful specialist even though its information is bounded. In a DIY system, that boundary helps players trust sensing and knowledge primitives: the benefit they bought is real, while interpretation remains something characters and people must do.

sections.title: Prepare a correction people can witness
sections.text:
Write a simple timeline: the courier reached the kiln before dawn; the potter accepted the coat after the courier left; the neighbor saw a separate figure enter from the river lane. Give each statement a source. The neighbor can be mistaken about appearance without invalidating the kiln’s physical evidence. This keeps the investigation from hinging on one absolute truth roll.

Player: “We tell the handler the scent only proves the coat was here.” DM: “He asks why the courier would leave it.” Player: “We invite the potter to show the broken fastening and ask the neighbor about the visitor.” The exchange introduces evidence and a possible explanation. If the handler still doubts it, identify the particular doubt rather than rolling to erase all suspicion.

A quiet correction may release the potter but leave customers believing the original accusation. A public correction can change that wider consequence, while requiring the party to admit their part if they joined the threat. Write down which correction happened. Later help from the potter can reflect the actual relationship. This gives investigation a social aftermath without requiring a town-wide reputation score or rewarding accusation merely because it made the session move faster.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Bellwatch Hound following a worn coat through a crowded lane, with its handler visibly studying the same trail. The illustration should emphasize a physical scent source and the possibility of a transferred object, rather than supernatural detection of guilt.

quickFacts.value: A scent attached to a coat

quickFacts.label: Uncertainty
quickFacts.value: What happened to the courier and how the coat moved

quickFacts.label: Consequence
quickFacts.value: A particular person’s changed access or trust, with an ending condition

modules.title: Keep the work and its price separate
modules.kicker: Original example · Ongoing consequences

sections.title: Describe what must continue
sections.text:
A Null Choir Node occupies an enclosed rehearsal room. Read its actual Chamber Blackout Matrix before deciding which light or senses are affected. In this example a party member has an approved capability that keeps a narrow exit lamp burning while they sing. The party agreed that singing and remaining beside its source are this working’s ongoing requirements.

The character can use the illuminated route without gaining a permanent Light primitive from the scene. The Node’s appearance supplies no additional silence, counterspell or blindness beyond its record. Establish which people can currently locate the exit and what happens if the lamp ends. An observable source makes interruption and protection meaningful.

sections.title: Agree a cost that fits the action
sections.text:
Player: “Can I brighten the whole room?” DM: “Your present working keeps the exit lit. A larger expression would change the scale. Are you trying to maintain a safe route or remove all the chamber’s darkness?” Player: “Keep the route. I will stay here while the others reach the control.”

That choice can use a restrictive consequence rather than damage. Record the subject, requirement, continuation point and ending condition. Maintaining one capability has one execution, one Strain appraisal and one upkeep track by default, even if it contains several effects. Multiple maintained capabilities have their actual requirements; no automatic single-concentration limit is imported.

sections.title: Let interference have a cause
sections.text:
If the singer leaves the source or becomes unable to sing, apply the agreed terms. If a hostile action destroys the lamp, use that physical change. A hit that does neither is not a universal cancellation command. Injury can matter through the real consequence, the character’s actual ability and the working’s rule.

The additional Vitality repayment triggered by incoming damage, including threshold, counter window, reset and excess treatment, remains pending in v0.1 alpha. This scene does not settle it. If your table uses a temporary treatment, identify it as your agreement. Ordinary recurring payments, tasks, restrictions and narrative obligations remain available without that unresolved numerical scheme.

sections.title: Do not wipe the price at Council
sections.text:
At the next Council, review the lamp’s agreed requirement. The new round does not erase the need to sing or release an obligation acquired elsewhere. If the room is opened and daylight now supplies the route, the party can end the lamp deliberately. Describe that new circumstance rather than keeping the upkeep active merely because a box remains marked.

Afterward, record whether the singer can redirect that capability, whether any separate consequence remains and who has reached safety. A continuing working is easier to run when its actual task is visible. The drama comes from protecting or replacing the source, not from forcing every form of upkeep into the same damage counter.

sections.title: Prepare a replacement before the source ends
sections.text:
Draw the exit lamp, the performer’s position and a shutter that can admit ordinary daylight. Decide what blocks access to the shutter and what the Node’s actual matrix changes. The party can then pursue a replacement source or a different route while the performer keeps the present route usable. The required singing is an agreed task, not a universal restriction on all maintained work.

Player: “I keep singing while they move the stool to the shutter.” DM: “You remain beside the lamp. The stool now makes the latch reachable.” Player: “Once daylight reaches the exit, I stop.” DM: “Then your lamp ends under its agreed terms; describe whether the new light actually supplies the needed route.” A completed setup gives a reason to release a continuing obligation.

If the shutter is jammed, the stool is still useful and the lamp still works while its requirements are met. If the lamp ends first, the party’s positions and knowledge of the latch remain. Do not reset all work to the chamber’s initial state. Record any separate lingering injury or promise independently. The next attempt should begin from the room the players changed, not from an invisible upkeep counter whose unresolved alpha details were silently chosen for them.

modules.title: Price the promise you actually wrote
modules.kicker: Original example · Reviewing a new primitive

sections.title: Begin with the claimed change
sections.text:
A player is inspired by the Mnemonic Surgeon and proposes a primitive called Steady Counsel. Their first draft says, “Restore anyone’s confidence and remove mental harm.” The creature’s actual Kindly, Collect Yourself is useful inspiration, but its existence does not define that broad new statement. Ask which result the player wants to acquire.

They clarify: add a qualifying bonus to one named practice while the recipient follows a short spoken instruction. That is a narrower numerical benefit than changing beliefs, restoring Vitality or removing every mental consequence. The original title may stay, but the actual rule must identify recipient, metric, operation, condition and limits before price can be meaningfully reviewed.

sections.title: Compare two distinct revisions
sections.text:
One revision grants training in a practice. Another adds a flat numerical bonus to qualifying practice checks. Those operations are different. A training grant does not repeatedly add PB to someone who already has the relevant training, while an actual numerical addition can stack under its authored rules. State which revision the player intends.

DM: “Does this teach the practice, or improve a particular use of it?” Player: “Improve it while the instruction is being followed.” DM: “Then name what following means, and whether a recording qualifies.” A condition should be answerable at the table. “When inspired” is unclear unless the group defines what establishes and ends that state.

sections.title: Judge the authored cost openly
sections.text:
The player selects a BU price. Library anchors can inform that choice; they are not a compulsory tariff. Review how often the rule can qualify, how many recipients it can affect and whether multiple occurrences can accumulate. A narrow single-recipient condition can differ from an always-on party benefit even when both add the same number.

If the price seems wrong for the campaign, explain the behavior that concerns you and request a revised price or narrower rule. Do not accept the broad version privately, then reinterpret it mid-scene to avoid its strength. Approval concerns the actual construction and its agreed price, not whether its name resembles an existing official option.

sections.title: Try the edge before approval
sections.text:
Test three situations: ordinary use with the recipient attending; a second support source applying simultaneously; and a recipient who cannot hear the instruction. Resolve each from the draft. If the answers are missing, finish the definition before purchase. This small review is more useful than an arbitrary catalogue of every possible abuse.

The Surgeon’s own conditional Reason bonus applies only where its actual rule says it does. Its portrait and support identity do not authorize free recovery or unlimited information. Keep that same discipline for the player’s inspiration. A DIY creation becomes dependable when another person can read its effect and reach the same result, while its price remains an openly negotiated authoring choice.

sections.title: Run the review as a short rehearsal
sections.text:
Use a deliberately ordinary scene: one recipient repairs a buckle while the counselor gives a spoken instruction. Ask the author to identify the exact qualifying practice and numerical operation. Then add a second counselor, a recorded instruction and a recipient who has walked beyond hearing. These changes test the definition without requiring a simulated boss fight.

Player: “The recording should qualify because the words are the same.” DM: “Then the condition is hearing the instruction, not receiving live counsel. Are you comfortable with it continuing whenever that recording is used?” Player: “No; I want a particular exchange with one present counselor.” Rewrite that choice into the rule and revisit the authored price. The conversation has revealed the benefit’s real frequency.

Compare the original and revised promises side by side. “Restore anyone’s confidence” could imply removed consequences, altered beliefs and unlimited recipients. The revised qualifying bonus claims none of those unless separately acquired. Keep the evocative name and explanation if they help, but read the precise claim when approving a scene. A small rehearsal protects the creator’s intended concept while giving other players a reliable boundary they can recognize.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Mnemonic Surgeon addressing one distressed subject across an ordinary workbench, with its tools set aside. The composition should make a bounded support exchange clear and avoid implying that the creature reads or rewrites every mind nearby.

quickFacts.value: Training grant or actual numerical addition?
