quickFacts.value: Frequency, recipients, stacking and restrictions

quickFacts.label: Approval test
quickFacts.value: Ordinary use, a second source and a failed condition

modules.title: A reference is not another purchase
modules.kicker: Original example · Shared acquisitions and equipment

sections.title: Separate what is owned from where it appears
sections.text:
A Silkgear Patchwright works on a damaged caravan. Its actual Patch the Seam provides the relevant repair behavior. A player who studies it wants to organize their own acquired rules into a heritage, a reusable effect and a capability. They place the same owned Verb I reference into all three.

That is organizational reuse, not three purchases of Verb I. One actual acquisition is counted once in the character’s acquired BU even when it appears in several containers or is used directly. If the player deliberately buys another eligible occurrence, that is a distinct acquisition with its own scope and stacking terms. The ledger must distinguish those two situations.

sections.title: Read the organizations back aloud
sections.text:
Player: “My heritage contains Repairer’s Habit. My Seam effect uses it, and the capability uses the effect.” DM: “Which underlying acquisitions do you own?” Player: “This Verb permission and these other rules.” DM: “Then those bought records are the ledger. The names organize them.”

A capability can also contain primitives directly. An effect is useful when it groups reusable ingredients; it is not required before every capability. A heritage explains a natural organization of acquired content. None of those labels automatically grants an extra repair, a second Main Intent or another numerical copy. Read actual contributions after identifying the owned occurrences.

sections.title: Keep the carried tool separate
sections.text:
The Patchwright’s mundane needles can be equipment without extraordinary Item BU. A tool containing its own acquired extraordinary rule uses a separate item acquisition ledger. Do not include that item’s rule twice by also treating its granted behavior as another paid character acquisition unless the character genuinely owns a separate instance.

Load, equipped slots, Item BU and ordinary value remain different measurements. An ordinary equipped item uses one slot; a two-handed item uses two unless its authored requirement says otherwise. An expensive artisan tool need not have a high Item BU. Conversely, a cheap-looking tool can carry a powerful acquired rule. Its appearance cannot settle those figures.

sections.title: Verify a scene from the ledger
sections.text:
Ask the player to repair a coat, a cracked wagon frame and a living wound. The first two may be ordinary or extraordinary tasks supported by actual material and verb access. The third is a different subject and result; organizing every rule under “Repairer” does not supply Life access or healing.

Use the caravan scene to expose missing permissions before purchase or revision. If the broad claim was accidental, rewrite it without charging organizational labels as mechanics. Afterward, the reader should be able to point to the actual owned rules, separate equipment costs and one declared working. Clean accounting makes flexible construction easier, rather than forcing every concept into a fixed class package.

sections.title: Mark the same acquisition with the same identity
sections.text:
Prepare a paper example with three boxes labeled heritage, effect and capability. Put one acquired Verb I record beside them and draw references from that same record into the appropriate boxes. Then place a second genuinely purchased record beside it with its own identity. The first drawing shows reuse; the second shows an additional acquisition that needs its own review.

Player: “The Seam effect already includes my permission, so adding it to the capability costs me again?” DM: “Which new rule did you acquire?” Player: “None. I am using the same one.” DM: “Then the organization changed, not the acquired ledger.” If another trait genuinely contributes a separate modifier, identify that contribution rather than hiding it beneath the repeated name.

For an item, draw a separate ledger and show which behavior it grants while equipped. Compare the character with the item, without it and with a second eligible owned source. Those three cases reveal accidental double counting and actual stacking questions. The Patchwright’s repair scene is a useful test because ordinary tools can help without necessarily having Item BU, while an extraordinary tool’s acquired rule must still be accounted for once in its own place.

modules.imagePurpose: Show the Silkgear Patchwright repairing a caravan seam, with one identifiable tool and one repeated stitch motif. Beside it, the design can trace a single acquired ingredient into several organizations; the illustration’s repeated marks must not look like multiple bought copies.

quickFacts.value: One bought record, counted once

quickFacts.label: Organization
quickFacts.value: Heritage, effect or capability can reference it

quickFacts.label: Equipment
quickFacts.value: Extraordinary item acquisitions have separate Item BU

modules.title: Build the injury, not a species stereotype
modules.kicker: Original example · Creating a creature from a purpose

sections.title: Choose the problem before the powers
sections.text:
A Saltwound Leviathan blocks a shipping route because its injured flank makes the deeper channel painful. Sailors call it a destroyer. The party can see an old harpoon, cautious movement and boats crowding a shallow passage. Its published concept supports treatment or diversion as meaningful approaches.

Begin your creature design with that purpose. Decide what the creature wants, what it can notice and which behavior creates the problem. Its saved Driving Blow supplies a particular attack; Cold Resistance supplies its actual defense. A sea-giant appearance does not provide every water domain, unlimited swimming, automatic drowning or a second action. Add a necessary mechanic explicitly rather than concealing it in the narration.

sections.title: Choose the budget, then construct
sections.text:
Select the creature’s base budget for the intended campaign and calculate its foundation through the existing creature procedure. Rank supplies attribute points and the other foundation references; allocate them to the actual focus you want. Then acquire the permissions, practices, expressions and structural rules that support its behavior.

Do not treat unspent budget as an invisible reserve of powers. A creature can have remaining BU without gaining an emergency ability when the party finds a weakness. If an extraordinary piece of equipment matters, price it separately as Item BU. Appraise the chosen base budget, not merely the sum currently spent on its acquisitions.

sections.title: Check one attack and one alternative
sections.text:
Run the actual Driving Blow from its record: eligible target, delivery, check or resistance procedure, output and consequences. Then test an approach that is not an attack. Could the party remove the harpoon with ordinary tools? What position and uncertainty make that dangerous? Does the creature understand an offered diversion, or must someone establish communication?

DM: “It turns away when the chain pulls the wound.” Player: “I want to slacken the chain before approaching.” DM: “That changes the source of pain. How are you reaching the fastening?” Their plan has found a concrete lever. Do not answer by inventing immunity to treatment because the creature was intended as a solo fight.

sections.title: Keep the creature useful after the scene
sections.text:
If the wound is treated, the Leviathan may leave the shipping route. If diverted without treatment, it might later occupy another passage. If defeated, the harbor has a carcass, a disputed harpoon and people claiming credit. Each outcome can generate different future material.

Record the actual creature changes independently from the template. A play copy can keep an injury, a relationship or a location; those do not rewrite every creature of that kind. A good monster definition supports repeatable mechanics, while this encounter’s history supplies individuality. That lets one evocative portrait serve a real situation without pretending that its illustration is an exhaustive bestiary rule.

sections.title: Write the next appearance from the first outcome
sections.text:
Before play, note the harpoon’s owner, the wound’s accessible fastening and the shipping channel that the Leviathan avoids. These facts can explain its present behavior. They also give the party something to change besides a Vitality total. Keep any proposed treatment within its actual subject, permissions and practical access.

Player: “If we slacken the chain, it can move without that pull.” DM: “The chain stops dragging the wound when it turns. It can still feel the embedded head.” Player: “Then we offer a route where we can approach the fastening safely.” That first achievement does not cure the whole injury, but it can create a new opportunity. A later effort should begin from the slackened chain.

If the party treats the wound, the creature’s next appearance may be in deeper water, passing boats without blocking them. If they divert it while leaving the chain, fishermen at the other channel may ask for help. If they fight, the harpoon’s owner may need to answer for the original injury. Record which history belongs to this play copy. Reusing the same template and portrait later can then reveal a changed relationship, rather than presenting a supposedly identical fresh obstacle.

modules.imagePurpose: Use the Saltwound Leviathan’s wounded silhouette beside small shipping craft, with a clear alternate channel. The scale conveys danger, while wound and route explain why treatment or diversion can matter. Do not add anatomical attack labels that the saved build does not contain.

quickFacts.value: Pain makes one channel unusable

quickFacts.label: Construction
quickFacts.value: Chosen base BU, actual acquisitions and separate equipment

quickFacts.label: Alternative
quickFacts.value: Treat, slacken, divert or confront the source of danger

modules.title: A warning must help someone choose
modules.kicker: Original example · Preparing a discoverable hazard

sections.title: Begin with a dangerous fact
sections.text:
A laboratory’s sealed chamber contains a Stillpoint Orb. Its actual Gravity Anchor Trap holds a prepared area. Before the party approaches, decide where that area is, what establishes its source and which visible evidence suggests the boundary. Loose fragments, a strained tether and a workbench outside the affected space are useful physical facts. The creature’s appearance does not settle the exact dimensions or operation; use the saved capability.

Put the laboratory’s missing attendant beyond a doorway adjoining the chamber. The party wants to reach them, not necessarily destroy the orb. Give the attendant a reason to remain: their trapped tool bag, a locked exit or fear of crossing the boundary. Pick the fact that makes this particular problem interesting, and show it when the party has a way to observe it.

sections.title: Make the warning actionable
sections.text:
A warning that only says “this place is dangerous” gives little help. Describe evidence that lets someone choose a route, prepare an approach or ask a useful question. The particles stop at a clear edge. The attendant’s tether bends toward the same place. A discarded inspection pole lies outside it. None of those observations requires a compulsory check when plainly visible.

Player: “I stay outside the fragments’ edge and use the pole to examine it.” DM: “What part are you touching, and what do you want to learn?” Player: “Whether the tether is caught on something physical.” Resolve that actual inquiry. An ordinary probe can reveal an ordinary fastening without granting knowledge of every magical mechanism. Extraordinary information still needs the relevant permissions and scope.

sections.title: Commit after the useful facts are available
sections.text:
If someone deliberately crosses the known boundary, state the relevant risk before resolving its trigger. They may accept it to reach the attendant. Do not add an unrelated explosion because the party ignored your preferred route. The trap does what its actual rule provides, and its source remains where you prepared it.

Player: “I can see the attendant, so I try to move them from here.” DM: “You know their location. Read the working’s subject, verb, reach and other permissions; knowing where they are does not by itself supply that movement.” The party can then choose an eligible working, an ordinary rescue through the area or a different route. This preserves the value of observation without allowing observation alone to solve the physical problem.

sections.title: Change only what the intervention changes
sections.text:
The party might move the source, alter an ordinary fastening, provide a new support or approach through the neighboring room. Resolve how each change interacts with the authored trap. Breaking a visible ring is not automatically a universal dispel. If you intend the ring to be essential, establish that dependency through the actual definition or the prepared physical situation.

Compare two outcomes. A successful rescue through the chamber can leave the containment active and the laboratory unsafe. Securing the source can make the route usable while the attendant remains trapped by a separate fastening. Mark both facts. If a probe fails, preserve its useful observation rather than making the entire chamber mysterious again. Future declarations should respond to the changed space and the information already obtained.

sections.title: Prepare a compact hazard record
sections.text:
Write five things in your notes: the actual working; its source; the visible boundary; the person or object at stake; and one nearby physical feature the party can investigate. This is enough to run a distinct scene without creating a new hazard subsystem. Leave the players room to propose means you did not anticipate.

After the rescue, ask the attendant what they actually know. They may explain the laboratory’s maintenance routine without knowing who changed the source. Their testimony can lead to another situation, but it should not retroactively supply perfect instructions they refused to give earlier. A broken inspection tool can be evidence of an earlier attempt without supplying a complete solution. The rescued attendant may know who used it or where a replacement is stored. That gives the party another practical inquiry grounded in the laboratory they have changed.

modules.imagePurpose: The Stillpoint Orb’s nested rings and suspended fragments make the actual containment subject legible. Relate that portrait to a small plan showing the prepared boundary, its source and an accessible observation point; readers should see why inspecting the edge changes a decision.

quickFacts.label: Prepared record
quickFacts.value: Working, source, boundary, stake and nearby feature

quickFacts.label: Useful warning
quickFacts.value: An observation that can change route or preparation

quickFacts.label: After intervention
quickFacts.value: Preserve completed rescue and unresolved containment separately

modules.title: The hearing has three legitimate concerns
modules.kicker: Original example · Factions and testimony

sections.title: Give each group a specific concern
sections.text:
A repaired floodgate fails after the first heavy rain. The repair guild wants proof that the stonework was inspected. Residents want the gate made safe before another storm. Cargo owners want the blocked channel reopened. Their concerns can conflict without making one group secretly evil. Prepare who can speak for each group and which commitments that person is authorized to make.

A Waxseal Witness preserved an attendant’s testimony through its actual Witness Seal. That contribution is valuable, but it is not an all-knowing verdict on the accident. Decide what the attendant saw, what they inferred and what happened beyond their view. Those distinctions give the hearing material the party can investigate and prevent the construct from replacing every participant’s judgment.

sections.title: Keep the statement and its interpretation separate
sections.text:
The attendant says, “The western brace was installed before dusk.” The guild treats that as proof of a completed repair. Residents ask whether anyone checked its lower fastening. Cargo owners ask why the channel remained closed. One preserved statement can be accurate while answering none of those later questions.

Player: “We ask the Witness if the guild caused the failure.” DM: “Its actual contribution preserves this testimony. The statement describes installation, not the later inspection or the cause.” Player: “Then we ask to see the brace and hear from the inspector.” That request can open a concrete investigation. The construct’s conditional Reason benefit applies under its actual condition; it does not automatically confer authority over everyone present or certify the entire guild’s innocence.

sections.title: Let a concession address a real need
sections.text:
Prepare one offer each representative could reasonably accept. The guild can send a named mason to inspect the fastening. The residents can allow access through their courtyard if the work is supervised. The cargo owners can lend a lifting frame for the inspection. None of those concessions answers every dispute, but together they may permit the next useful task.

Player: “We will publish what the inspection finds, even if it clears the guild.” Resident: “And the gate stays shut until it is safe?” Player: “Until the inspection establishes a usable route or we agree an alternative.” The conversation names the actual undertaking and its boundary. Resolve uncertainty where distrust or conflicting interests remain. A credible shared plan may already answer a concern without requiring a roll to compel agreement.

sections.title: Show the changed hearing
sections.text:
If inspection finds a fastening deliberately removed, the guild’s installation claim can remain true while a new question appears. If it finds incomplete work, the preserved statement still establishes what the attendant witnessed. Do not turn every earlier speaker into a liar when one interpretation fails. Let the party compare the new physical evidence with the actual testimony.

A repair-first agreement can reopen the safe part of the channel while blame remains disputed. A blame-first confrontation may delay repair and change who cooperates. Record those outcomes without a universal faction score. Name the person who agreed to lend the frame, the people who heard the promise and the gate’s present condition. Later scenes can follow those particular commitments rather than an invisible reputation meter.

sections.title: Prepare the next relationship
sections.text:
After the hearing, ask each representative one useful question in your notes: what do they still need, and what did the party make possible? The mason might ask for an escort to the damaged footing. Residents might offer shelter because the party kept the inspection public. Cargo owners might dispute the cost of delays while still honoring the loan.

Player: “We thought reopening the channel ended this.” DM: “The safe route is open. The frame must still be returned, and the missing fastening remains unexplained.” That distinction creates continuity without declaring a new quest by force. The party can fulfill, renegotiate or knowingly break the promise. The Witness remains useful when the content and provenance of testimony matter. Its artwork can anchor the hearing visually while the surrounding text gives the three groups recognizable, different stakes.

modules.imagePurpose: The Waxseal Witness’s civic form belongs beside a hearing involving protected testimony. Its wax tools and careful posture should introduce the difference between preserving a statement and deciding whether that statement proves a wider claim.

quickFacts.label: Factions
quickFacts.value: Guild: inspection; residents: safety; cargo owners: access

quickFacts.label: Evidence
quickFacts.value: Preserved testimony has a particular speaker and subject

quickFacts.label: Continuity
quickFacts.value: Named commitments and changed physical conditions

modules.title: Say the promise before accepting it
modules.kicker: Original example · Negotiation and continuing obligations

sections.title: Make the offer intelligible
sections.text:
A Velvet Oath Broker offers passage into a district closed after an arcane accident. In exchange, it wants a seal returned from the abandoned counting house. The Broker has its actual The Open Door Argument, not unlimited compulsion. Its presence, portrait and title do not make every spoken sentence a magically binding contract.

Prepare the offered access, the named seal and the Broker’s reason for wanting it. Decide what the Broker knows about the counting house and what it does not. If danger is known, the party should have a fair chance to inquire before accepting. A bargain can be tense because its benefits and obligations matter, without depending on a hidden pun that rewrites the players’ ordinary understanding after agreement.

sections.title: Clarify who owes what
sections.text:
Player: “We bring it back if it is there.” Broker: “Then I offer entry for your search, not a promise of return?” Player: “Yes. We will make a good-faith search and report what happened.” This changes the bargain. Make the accepted version explicit rather than keeping two contradictory promises in your notes.

State who receives passage, whether it lasts for one visit and how the district’s physical gate works. State who must search, what counts as the requested seal and where a report can be delivered. These are practical terms, not a compulsory contract-building subsystem. If a capability imposes an actual consequence or restriction, read it separately. Mundane agreement, authored argumentative effects and extraordinary binding are different claims with different permissions.

sections.title: Let persuasion have a subject
sections.text:
The Broker may press for a more favorable bargain through its actual argument. Identify the proposition and the applicable procedure. Someone agreeing that the seal matters has not automatically agreed to surrender every possession or abandon a companion. Resolve the actual influence and preserve the character’s available choices under the rule.

Player: “I show that the district’s people need the gate reopened, not just us.” DM: “The Broker can authorize your entry. It does not control the entire cordon.” Player: “Then we ask it to speak with the gatekeepers too.” That proposed extension needs another person’s authority or another eligible effect. Negotiation becomes useful when the table knows which decision each participant can actually make, rather than treating a powerful speaker as the owner of every related outcome.

sections.title: Compare two discoveries
sections.text:
If the seal is intact, returning it can satisfy an actual return promise. If it was melted into a repair plate, the party has found a changed subject. Whether the promise is still satisfiable depends on the agreed words and circumstances, not a concealed authorial trick. Give them evidence and an opportunity to report or negotiate a substitute.

A search-and-report bargain can be fulfilled despite a failed recovery. A return bargain may remain unresolved until the Broker accepts the evidence or a replacement. Record the continuing consequence’s subject, requirement and ending condition. It need not become recurring damage. Do not clear the promise merely because a new Council begins, and do not extend it to unrelated people who never accepted or were never affected by an actual rule.

sections.title: Prepare the account after the bargain
sections.text:
Write the accepted promise in one sentence the players recognize. Add the benefit already received and the event that would end the obligation. For this example: the Broker admitted the named group for one visit; they owe a search and truthful report about the seal; the report ends that agreed obligation. Another table might choose a different bargain, but the record should be equally clear.

Player: “We found the plate and brought its maker as a witness.” Broker: “I asked about the seal. Show me why this answers.” The resulting exchange can change the relationship through particular facts. A fulfilled bargain may make the Broker a future contact; an honest failed search may reveal a better offer; a knowingly broken promise may close that offered access. Keep those outcomes rooted in the agreement, not a universal debt score or automatic moral judgment.

modules.imagePurpose: Use the Velvet Oath Broker’s contract-bearing silhouette to frame a bounded negotiation. Place the entry being offered and the promise being requested together in the spread’s composition, so the reader connects elegance and temptation to actual terms rather than assumed supernatural compulsion.

quickFacts.label: Offer
quickFacts.value: Named passage for an explicit search or return promise

quickFacts.label: Authority
quickFacts.value: Each negotiator can commit only what they control

quickFacts.label: Ending condition
quickFacts.value: Record the event that satisfies the agreed obligation

modules.title: Three routes to one necessary fact
modules.kicker: Original example · Clues and practical adventure preparation

sections.title: Choose the conclusion the adventure needs
sections.text:
The party needs to learn that a sealed archive has an older entrance through a repair chamber. That fact opens useful choices; it does not prescribe how they enter. Prepare the old chamber’s actual location and why the newer door was sealed. Then build several independent ways to discover the entrance from those facts.

Visible masonry shows a patched arch. A maintenance record names the chamber’s access passage. A Stone Script Reader can offer evidence through its actual Mineral Recollection. These routes should not all depend on the same unavailable witness or identical failed check. Each has a distinct provenance and a limit. The Reader’s ability concerns its authored subject and scope, not every event in the building’s complete history.

sections.title: Make observation different from interpretation
sections.text:
Someone examining the outer wall can see different mortar when the conditions allow it. What that patch signifies may remain uncertain. The maintenance record can establish that a passage existed without proving its present safety. An eligible recollection can show an actual repair within its rule while leaving later changes unknown.

Player: “The patch means the archive is behind this wall.” DM: “It shows a repaired arch here. The record names a chamber beyond it; you have not inspected that chamber.” Player: “Then I compare the arch’s location with the passage diagram.” The comparison uses available information to narrow the question. Give accessible observations clearly and choose a check only for a meaningful uncertainty, rather than charging a roll for every sentence of description.

sections.title: A failed route can change the approach
sections.text:
If the party cannot read the maintenance script, the masonry still exists and the Reader may still be approachable. If the Reader refuses a request because the party damaged a slab, that relationship changes; it does not make the archive’s old entrance vanish. Prepare what the refusal actually means and what could repair the relationship.

Failure can cost an opportunity, alert someone to the investigation or leave a narrower question unresolved when those stakes were established. It need not produce false certainty that stops the adventure. Avoid repeatedly asking for the same roll until success appears. A changed means, new evidence or a new relationship can justify a fresh inquiry because the actual situation differs, not because another player touched the same wall.

sections.title: Prepare a useful answer, not a lecture
sections.text:
Give the Reader one piece of information that advances the investigation and one honest limit. It recalls a repair crew closing the lower passage before the flood. It does not know whether the passage was reopened later. That is enough to make the next physical inspection meaningful.

Player: “Who ordered the repair?” DM: “The recollection identifies the crew’s mark, but this trace does not establish the order’s author.” Player: “We follow the crew’s records.” The distinction opens another line of inquiry without inventing a broader information power. If your selected capability genuinely answers more, honor that benefit. Do not artificially narrow a purchased rule because the prepared mystery would otherwise be solved too quickly; let an early answer change the adventure’s remaining questions.

sections.title: Write what the party knows now
sections.text:
At the end of the scene, separate three statements in your notes: the entrance existed; its access passage was closed before the flood; its present condition is unknown. Mark which characters heard or saw each source. These are preparation notes, not a mandatory evidence-tracking mechanic. They help the next scene begin with understandable choices.

The party might excavate, request permission from the archive’s keeper or follow the crew’s route through the cellar. Each approach uses the same established fact differently. If the chamber is flooded, their information was not worthless; it changed the route they chose and the equipment they can prepare. If the party returns to the Reader with that new observation, it can compare the finding with its actual recollection. A flooded passage and a remembered closure can both be true. Together they identify a more precise question: what changed the chamber after the crew left?

modules.imagePurpose: The Stone Script Reader’s mosaic hands, worn slab and repair wheel explain evidence with physical provenance. Use the portrait beside a simple relationship of observation, maintenance record and authored recollection; the art supports material memory without implying omniscience.

quickFacts.value: An older entrance passes through a repair chamber

quickFacts.label: Record distinctly
quickFacts.value: Observation, interpretation and unresolved present condition

modules.title: A journey can change before anyone attacks
modules.kicker: Original example · Travel and competing attention

sections.title: Prepare the reason for pursuit
sections.text:
A caravan crosses a dry woodland with grain spilling from a torn sack. Thornpath Jackals follow the food trail and watch for separated travelers. Their actual Driving Blow and climbing benefit support their published behavior; a pack identity does not give them shared Vitality, invisible coordination or free attacks whenever someone looks away.

Draw the route, a stopping place and the root-covered ground beside it. Decide when the caravan discovers the tear and how the animals respond to people approaching. The immediate problem can be protecting food and keeping travelers together. It does not require an obligatory battle. Give the jackals a plausible reason to withdraw, such as food obtained elsewhere or losing the opportunity to approach safely, without pretending every hungry animal understands a spoken negotiation.

sections.title: Offer information that makes preparation worthwhile
sections.text:
The party can see grain behind the rear cart and shapes moving along the roots. A driver knows that the next bend narrows the route. Those observations let the players choose whether to repair the sack, reorganize the caravan or keep watch from another position. Ordinary work can remove an ordinary source of risk when time, tools and access permit it.

Player: “We stop before the bend and repack the grain.” DM: “Who watches the rear while the drivers unload?” Player: “I stay with them; the other two check the tear.” This is a useful distribution of attention. It is not automatically a new Main Intent for everyone or a mandatory timed challenge. Use the shared round when interacting timing or interference makes it useful, rather than converting every minute of travel into Council.

sections.title: Compare three approaches
sections.text:
Guarding the rear may discourage an approach while the grain continues to spill. Repairing the sack removes that trail but requires a stopping place. Taking the open ridge changes the route and may leave the injured traveler with a harder climb. Establish the relevant facts, then let the party propose how to address them.

Player: “We move onto the ridge.” DM: “The carts can follow the longer track. The injured traveler cannot use the steep shortcut without help.” Player: “Then we keep everyone on the cart route and carry the torn sack separately.” Their plan combines means grounded in the scene. Do not impose a universal travel consequence merely because they avoided combat; apply the actual work, delay or exposure their chosen approach creates.

sections.title: If the pack attacks, keep creatures independent
sections.text:
Mark each jackal’s position and actual state. A member climbing the roots can use its real movement; another attacking a traveler resolves its own eligible action. Their role suggests what they try, while their actual records determine what they can do. Several creatures do not become one creature merely because they share a portrait and tactic.

For encounter appraisal, multiply each template’s chosen base BU by its quantity and keep extraordinary Item BU separate. Do not appraise only the acquisitions spent, and do not infer an automatic difficulty from the combined total. Terrain, information, exposed travelers and the party’s preparation can change the practical threat substantially. A successful repair can matter even if the eventual creature count and nominal budgets remain the same.

sections.title: Carry the journey’s changes forward
sections.text:
If the party saves the grain but abandons a damaged cart, the next settlement receives food and still has a recovery problem. If they leave food to distract the pack, note what was left and who accepted that choice. If a traveler is injured, their actual recovery need continues; the scene’s end does not restore Vitality or erase a consequence.

Driver: “You kept them off us. We can leave the last sack.” Player: “We agreed to bring all the grain, so we want to come back for it.” DM: “Then the caravan can reach shelter first. What will you need for the return?” That exchange turns travel into a changed situation and a meaningful promise. The pack’s next appearance can follow its actual behavior, while the caravan’s records preserve what the players accomplished and chose to risk.

modules.title: Rest begins with safe enough circumstances
modules.kicker: Original example · Shelter, recovery and continuing duties

sections.title: Prepare the people already inside
sections.text:
A Rootbound Aegis guards a sanctuary occupied by injured refugees. Its actual Doorway Brace supports the threshold; it does not automatically make the whole building invulnerable or grant its inhabitants recovery. The party arrives tired, carrying a rescued worker and seeking a place to sleep. The refugees need space, quiet and help moving supplies away from the exposed door.

Prepare the occupied rooms, the usable entrance and the threat the guardian expects. Decide who can grant hospitality and what assistance they request. The Aegis can protect a threshold without controlling every decision inside. A sanctuary becomes a real place when its safety comes from people, geography and actual work, not from a label that resets all character state on entry.

sections.title: Agree what the pause earns
sections.text:
Player: “We stay here for half an hour and take a short rest.” DM: “The occupants will offer that pause if the worker is settled and the entrance remains watched. Is that what the group agrees to do?” Player: “Yes; two of us help them, and I take the first watch.” Clarify whose actual circumstances support recovery. Performing a duty is not automatically the same experience as resting.

Short and long rests are table agreements about circumstances. A short pause may be fifteen or thirty minutes; overnight sleep need not be exactly eight hours. Elapsed time alone does not apply the effects. When a rest is agreed, use the character’s available recovery, with all ordinary rounding upward. Keep the source of safety and any unresolved treatment need visible.

sections.title: Use the actual remaining allowance
sections.text:
The ordinary short-rest allowance is half maximum Vitality, rounded up, available across eligible short rests until the next agreed long rest. Healing consumes only what is restored; unused allowance remains available. A character already at full Vitality does not need to spend the balance simply because everyone else pauses. A long rest’s recovery is independent and refreshes that short-rest pool.

A tired character may sleep poorly because they are watching the entrance or because the shelter is disturbed. The table can agree a partial long-rest recovery that fits the circumstances. For example, the DM may propose 70% of maximum Vitality for an interrupted night. Identify that as the group’s particular agreement, not a universal five-hour formula. Also clarify whether the agreed rest includes the ordinary long-rest refresh.

sections.title: Do not make hospitality an invisible trap
sections.text:
The refugees can ask the party to keep weapons away from children, help carry water or avoid fire near the dry roof. State those conditions when they matter. If someone violates one, describe the changed access or trust and what could repair it. A host’s frustration does not secretly invalidate every point of healing already resolved.

Player: “I leave to examine the noise outside.” DM: “You stop resting and take that task. The others remain inside; the guardian still holds the entrance.” The outside investigation can change the actual safety of the group, but do not automatically apply one character’s interruption to everyone. If an attack or another event disrupts the shelter, resolve it from positions and knowledge. The Aegis uses its actual working; the refugees do not acquire its defense by standing nearby.

sections.title: Open the next morning from the changed place
sections.text:
Record who completed an eligible rest, what Vitality was actually restored and which consequences remain. Lost access until treatment, a promise to return a borrowed sling and a damaged roof are different subjects; none vanishes merely because someone slept. Record whether the refugees can now move and whether the guarded entrance remains the useful route.

Refugee: “We can leave if someone carries the water.” Player: “We thought we were only staying the night.” DM: “You are rested under the agreement. Their journey is a new choice, not a hidden rest price.” The party may help, decline or negotiate another arrangement. The morning should reveal the benefits of the night’s actual work and the world’s continuing needs. A rest scene can strengthen relationships while keeping recovery understandable and free of retroactive penalties.

modules.imagePurpose: The Rootbound Aegis’s shield, roots and sanctuary threshold establish protection as a task performed in a particular place. Place its portrait near the shelter’s entrance plan and rest record, connecting the guardian’s role to what permits recovery rather than implying automatic healing.

modules.title: Prepare facts that survive a failed approach
modules.kicker: Original example · An adventure from premise to aftermath

sections.title: Start with a problem people care about
sections.text:
A district’s repair contract has disappeared. Without proof of who promised materials, the residents and workshop disagree about finishing a damaged bridge. A Ledger-Eater Imp has taken records into a hiding place. Its actual The Quiet Compartment supplies a particular concealment trick; the name alone does not erase contracts, devour all written evidence or create unlimited magical storage.

Write the situation’s stable facts: what the bridge needs, who made the promise, where a copy or witness could exist and what the Imp wants. Give the residents and workshop different immediate concerns. One needs a crossing; the other fears paying twice. The adventure begins when the party sees the damaged crossing and hears a disputed promise, not when an outline orders them to enter a particular cellar.

sections.title: Connect places by useful information
sections.text:
Prepare three reachable places: the workshop with its delivery record, the clerk’s room with evidence of the missing contract and the Imp’s hiding place. Connect them through facts characters can observe or obtain. A torn receipt can identify the workshop. A clerk can explain the last known location. A physical trail can lead toward the hiding place when the actual circumstances support it.

Player: “We talk to the workshop before chasing the thief.” DM: “The forewoman has a delivery record but no signed agreement. She asks what the residents can show.” That approach can establish part of the promise without finding the original. Each location should change the party’s understanding or options. A place that supplies only another compulsory check to reach the next compulsory check is not yet a useful scene.

sections.title: Prepare the opponent’s present choices
sections.text:
Give the Imp a reason to keep records: leverage, fascination or a mistaken belief that the promises inside will protect it. Choose one that fits the creature and your situation. Determine what it can perceive outside its actual compartment and how it could bargain. Its existing concealment gives a practical obstacle, while physical access and ordinary conversation remain possible where the scene permits them.

Player: “We offer a blank ledger for the contract.” DM: “It wants a record of a promise, not empty pages.” Player: “Then we record our promise to repair its torn satchel.” That offer can change the negotiation. If the Imp rejects it, the rejection should follow its motive or evidence. It need not automatically accept every clever phrase, and it should not gain a new immunity whenever a bargain threatens your planned chase.

sections.title: Let a failed approach leave another route
sections.text:
The party might fail to recover the original yet obtain a witness to its terms, locate a copy or negotiate a new agreement. Prepare those possibilities from the situation’s actual people and records. They need not produce an identical outcome. A new agreement can reopen the bridge while changing who bears the cost. A witness may settle one disputed delivery but leave another uncertain.

Compare that with a confrontation that retrieves the contract intact. The original obligation can be established, while the Imp’s reason for stealing remains a future issue. Failure to persuade the forewoman may close her cooperation for now but does not make the residents or clerk disappear. Carry consequences that were established; preserve the information the party earned. The story continues through changed means, rather than a hidden instruction that all roads must return to the cellar fight.

sections.title: Write an aftermath with actual owners
sections.text:
At the end, record the bridge’s condition, who accepted the repair agreement, where the contract is and what the party promised. These four facts give the next session useful material. If the party repaired the satchel but left the bridge unresolved, both facts remain true. If they restored the contract and refused further involvement, the residents can act with the evidence now available.

Player: “We solved the theft. Why is the workshop still angry?” DM: “You proved the promise, but you publicly accused the forewoman before checking her record.” The anger concerns the actual exchange; it is not punishment for finishing the adventure too quickly. A later apology, delivery or new cooperation can change it. Prepare people who can respond to the players’ real history, and the adventure will remain usable after an approach succeeds earlier, fails differently or is never attempted.

modules.imagePurpose: The Ledger-Eater Imp and its stolen records are the visual center of a practical preparation workshop. Use the contract, hiding place and repair need as related subjects around the portrait, demonstrating that a creature’s nuisance can connect people and routes without copying a predetermined adventure sequence.

modules.title: End with a place the players changed
modules.kicker: Original example · Session closing and campaign continuity

sections.title: Prepare an ending that can belong to several outcomes
sections.text:
An Ashwake Mourner remains near the burned home of its former companions. Its actual Splint and Rally makes support meaningful; undead flavor adds no unlisted immunities, healing or knowledge. The party’s session involved rescuing a resident, recovering a family token and deciding whether the damaged roof could shelter anyone. Any of those efforts can change the Mourner’s reason to stay.

Prepare a few people who can react to those changes: the rescued resident, a neighbor with a spare room and the caretaker who remembers the former household. Do not decide in advance that the session must end with the creature defeated or appeased. The closing scene can acknowledge what happened while leaving the next practical choice open.

sections.title: Ask for a concrete account
sections.text:
In the last few minutes, summarize physical changes and unresolved obligations. The resident is conscious; the token is recovered; the roof remains unsafe. Ask the players to correct missing facts. This is especially useful after a long scene with independent support, continuing work and separate consequences. A completed rescue does not imply every injury was healed.

DM: “You can leave the resident with the neighbor, but the medicine you borrowed still belongs to the caretaker. Is someone promising to return it?” Player: “I am. We take it to the next settlement and bring back what remains.” Record that accepted promise in recognizable terms. If another player declines, preserve that distinction rather than converting the whole party into a compulsory debt. The Mourner’s response follows what it can perceive and its actual motive.

sections.title: Reward the change the campaign values
sections.text:
The table can agree rewards that fit the campaign: access to shelter, a useful contact, payment, extraordinary content or progression through the established procedure. Do not import a fixed experience tariff for rescuing someone or defeating a creature. Distinguish an ordinary reward from a new acquired rule and keep extraordinary item acquisitions separate from character BU.

Player: “Does the token grant us a new heritage?” DM: “It is the family’s recovered possession. If you want a mechanical gift connected to it, we should define and approve that acquisition rather than assume the token contains one.” This keeps an evocative reward meaningful without making every narrative object a hidden magic item. A promise of future training can become a later scene; it need not instantly supply an unreviewed capability.

sections.title: Make one unresolved question clear
sections.text:
Choose an unresolved question already created by play. Who started the fire? Where can the resident safely recover? Why did the caretaker keep an identical token? The question should arise from a fact or relationship, not a surprise threat inserted only to prevent the group from resting. Give the players the evidence they actually have and let them decide what matters next.

Player: “We want to ask the caretaker about the second token.” DM: “Then the next session can begin at the borrowed room when they visit.” Another group may pursue the fire’s source or leave town. Record that intended direction as a starting point, not an obligation. The Mourner can remain an ally, a stranger or an unresolved danger depending on the actual encounter history.

sections.title: Leave a restartable situation
sections.text:
If someone will miss the next session, agree how their character’s presence and current obligations are handled. Do not silently spend their recovery or change their sheet to fit a new opening. Note the party’s location, current Vitality where relevant, remaining short-rest allowance, equipment held, ongoing work and consequences that matter next. This is a practical continuity record, not another campaign subsystem.

Open the following session with a changed fact the players recognize: the neighbor has cleared a bed; the caretaker arrives for the borrowed medicine; the Mourner now stands near the recovered token. Ask what the characters do from there. The last scene’s choices should still exist in the first scene’s world. A campaign gains coherence when shelter, injury, trust and completed work persist, even when the next adventure changes scale or the group revisits an old place months later.

Pair it with survivors, a recovered token or a quiet refuge only as the worked situation requires; the image’s purpose is to make care and a changed relationship visible.
